title: Tech Workers Have Long Resisted Unions. Will AI and Politics Change the Equation?
key_facts: As AI changes technical work, organizers say more Silicon Valley employees are reconsidering unions, though the idea is still unusual in the industry.

The Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Alphabet and Wikimedia, formed an AI advisory committee and released an AI bargaining toolkit; Wikimedia white-collar workers voted to unionize in September and Blizzard Entertainment ratified a union contract, both drives mentioning AI usage.
Workers cite fears of 'token tracking' (counting how often each employee uses AI) in performance reviews, and a shift from making decisions to 'shoveling data'.

A Stanford 2026 AI Index report found one-third of organizations surveyed expect more job cuts and that employment for entry-level software developers fell 20% from 2024; layoffs.fyi shows a rise in layoffs directly attributed to AI this year.

Alphabet Workers Union members run a Googlers Against ICE campaign against Google's partnerships with federal immigration agencies; it reached 1,700 signatures last month and was formally endorsed by the union. Google declined to comment.
The Alphabet Workers Union represents 'over a thousand' of roughly 190,000 Alphabet employees and is not yet registered with the National Labor Relations Board.
Only 3.7% of US workers in computer and mathematical occupations are unionized, against 10% across other industries (Bureau of Labor Statistics).
Lenny Siegel, former mayor of Mountain View, does not expect AI alone to push tech workers to unionize unless the AI bubble pops.
quote_evidence: Nationally, just 3.7% of workers in "computer and mathematical occupations" are unionized, compared to 10% of workers across other industries according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The idea of tech workers organizing collectively is still unusual in Silicon Valley.
Lenny Siegel, former mayor of Mountain View and a longtime activist, said that he does not believe AI alone will push tech workers to unionize.
why_it_matters_hint: AI anxiety is nudging some white-collar tech workers toward collective organizing, though union density in tech remains very low.
notes: Full text read. A feature built mostly on organizers' own accounts; no new union drive or decision reported.
